text: Azure Monitor isn't one dashboard — it's the platform underneath Log Analytics, Application Insights, Container Insights, and alerting alike. Everything else in this chapter and the next two builds on the same two underlying data stores: metrics and logs. Once you understand where each kind of telemetry actually lands, the rest of Azure's monitoring tooling stops feeling like a pile of unrelated products and starts looking like one consistent system.

Metrics live in a dedicated time-series database — numeric values on a timestamp, collected automatically for most resources roughly every minute, cheap enough to alert and dashboard on. Logs live in a Log Analytics workspace as structured tables, queried with KQL, able to carry full detail a metric has no room for. The Activity Log is the exception that needs no setup at all: a 90-day, subscription-level record of every control-plane operation, always on.

Here's the gap that trips up most teams: a resource's detailed data-plane logs don't automatically appear anywhere queryable. A diagnostic setting is the configuration object that routes a specific resource's log categories and metrics to a destination — a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an Event Hub. Skip that step, and a resource can look fully monitored while its most useful logs were never captured in the first place.

So which tool do you actually reach for? If the question is "is something wrong right now, across many resources," Metrics Explorer wins — fast, cheap, and able to scan dozens of resources in seconds. If the question is "what exactly happened, and can I slice it any way I want," that's a Log Analytics query — a few minutes of latency in exchange for joins, free-text filtering, and far richer detail.

Both can back an alert rule: a metric alert evaluates a numeric threshold on a fast cadence, while a log alert runs a scheduled KQL query for richer conditions at the cost of some latency. That's the map for this entire chapter. Next lesson goes hands-on with KQL itself — summarize, bin, render, and real joins across tables like AzureActivity and Perf, the actual queries you'd run on a live incident.
